newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN urges Tanzania not to use force against Rwandans.
newsitem.headline: UN urges Tanzania not to use force against Rwandans.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency appealed to Tanzania on Thursday not to use force against Rwandan refugees fleeing camps.

U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata has started urgent contacts with high-level Tanzanian officials which were expected to last late into the night, according to her spokeswoman in Geneva.

Tanzania had informed UNHCR that Rwandans outside a four-km (three-mile) parameter of camps were no longer refugees and were therefore subject to prosecution, according to the UNHCR spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole.
"UNHCR appeals to the Tanzanian authorities not to use force. UNHCR believes that these people are still refugees and should be treated as such," O'Toole told Reuters in Geneva.
At least 400,000 Rwandan refugees have abandoned their camps in northwestern Tanzania, voting with their feet against a plan to repatriate them by year-end, according to U.N. officials.
In Benaco refugee camp in Tanzania, once the largest in the country with 160,000 to 180,000 Rwandans, only a few stragglers lingered in the debris on Thursday afternoon.
U.N. officials in Tanzania said the five other camps in the area were also deserted, giving a total of between 400,000 and 500,000 people on the loose in the Tanzanian bush.
Many of the refugees were moving further inland, guided by their leaders, while some others said they were heading for Kenya, according to O'Toole.
The exodus started on a small scale last Sunday and began to snowball as word spread through the camps that refugees in other areas had struck camp and headed into the bush.

Members of the Hutu militia, the Interahamwe, do not want to go home for fear of prosecution or reprisals for the massacre of Rwandan Tutsis in 1994. They want the other refugees to stay with them on the grounds there is strength in numbers.
UNHCR had hoped it and the Tanzanians could persuade the refugees to go home willingly, following the example of more than 600,000 who have gone home from Zaire since mid-November.
